title: Parameters in depth
summary: Optional and named arguments, overloads, out and ref, params, and returning two things at once.

steps.title: Optional parameters and named arguments
body: Some arguments are the same nearly every time. Give the parameter a **default value** and callers may leave it out.
string Frame(string text, string edge = "*", int width = 2)
for (int i = 0; i < width; i++) side += edge;
Optional parameters must come **after** the required ones.
What if you want the default `edge` but your own `width`? Arguments are matched by position, so you cannot just skip one. Instead, **name** the parameter in the call:
Named arguments also make calls easier to read. `Resize(800, 600, true)` says little. `Resize(width: 800, height: 600, keepRatio: true)` explains itself.

steps.title: Two ways to show a duration
prompt: Your Sidekick already has two formatters from First steps: `Sk.FormatMinutes(minutes)` gives `1h 30m`, and `Sk.FormatDuration(seconds)` gives `1h 30m 00s`.

Write `static string Describe(int minutes, bool withSeconds = false)`. With the default it returns `Sk.FormatMinutes(minutes)`; with `withSeconds: true` it returns `Sk.FormatDuration` of the same time **in seconds**.
starter: static string Describe(int minutes, bool withSeconds = false)
solution: static string Describe(int minutes, bool withSeconds = false)
template: Dojo.Eq("Describe(90, withSeconds: true)", "1h 30m 00s", Describe(90, withSeconds: true));
Dojo.Eq("Describe(withSeconds: false, minutes: 125)", "2h 05m", Describe(withSeconds: false, minutes: 125));
hints: The default goes in the parameter list: `bool withSeconds = false`.
steps.explain: The last test passes both arguments by name and in the other order: named arguments make a call read like a sentence.

steps.title: Overloads: one name, several shapes
body: Have you noticed that `Console.WriteLine` accepts a string, an int, a double, or nothing at all? Those are four different methods that share one name. They are called **overloads**.
Console.WriteLine("text");  // the overload that takes a string
Console.WriteLine(42);      // the overload that takes an int
Console.WriteLine();        // the overload that takes nothing

The compiler picks the right one by looking at the **number and types of the arguments**. That is why overloads must differ in their parameter lists. A different return type alone is not enough: from the call `Parse("5")` nobody could tell which one you meant.
Overloads exist so callers do not have to remember `WriteLineInt`, `WriteLineString` and `WriteLineDouble`.

> **Tip:** you write your own overloads on methods inside a **class**, which comes in a later module. The standalone methods you write in these exercises cannot share a name, so for now use an optional parameter or pick a second name.

steps.prompt: Inside one class, which pair of methods can **not** live side by side as overloads?
options: `int Area(int side)` and `int Area(int width, int height)`
`void Log(string message)` and `void Log(string message, int level)`
steps.explain: The two `Parse` methods take exactly the same arguments and differ only in what they return. A call like `Parse("5")` could mean either, so the compiler rejects the pair.

steps.title: out and ref: reaching back to the caller
body: A parameter is normally a copy. Two keywords change that, and you have already used one of them:
`TryParse` has two things to report: *did it work?* and *what is the number?* It returns the first and delivers the second through an **`out` parameter**. You can write the same pattern yourself:
bool TryHalve(int n, out int half)
- `out` means *this parameter carries a result out*. The method **must** assign it before returning.
- The caller writes `out` too, so the hand-over is visible at the call.
`ref` is the two-way version. The method can read the caller's variable **and** change it:
void Double(ref int n) => n = n * 2;
Use these sparingly. A plain return value is easier to follow. `out` earns its place in the *Try* pattern, where failing is normal and not worth a crash.

steps.prompt: Complete the method so the `if` at the bottom prints `5`.
steps.explain: The call says `out`, so the parameter must be declared `out` as well. The `bool` answer goes back with `return`.

steps.title: Safe division
prompt: Dividing by zero crashes a program. Write a *Try* method that refuses politely instead:
`bool TryDivide(int a, int b, out int result)`
- When `b` is not zero: set `result` to `a / b` and return `true`.
- When `b` is zero: set `result` to `0` and return `false`.
starter: bool TryDivide(int a, int b, out int result)
// an out parameter must be given a value on every path
solution: bool TryDivide(int a, int b, out int result)
template: bool ok1 = TryDivide(10, 2, out int r1);
Dojo.Eq("TryDivide(10, 2, out r) returns true", true, ok1);
Dojo.Eq("TryDivide(10, 2, out r) sets r to 5", 5, r1);
bool ok2 = TryDivide(9, 4, out int r2);
Dojo.Eq("TryDivide(9, 4, out r) returns true", true, ok2);
Dojo.Eq("TryDivide(9, 4, out r) sets r to 2", 2, r2);
Dojo.Try("TryDivide(7, 0, out r) does not crash", () => { ok3 = TryDivide(7, 0, out r3); });
Dojo.Eq("TryDivide(7, 0, out r) returns false", false, ok3);
Dojo.Eq("TryDivide(7, 0, out r) sets r to 0", 0, r3);
hints: Every path must assign `result` before it returns, even the failing one.
`if (b == 0) { result = 0; return false; }` then `result = a / b; return true;`

steps.title: params: as many as you like
body: Sometimes you cannot know how many arguments a caller will have. Mark the **last** parameter with `params` and they may pass any number, including none.

`int[]` is an **array** of ints: a row of values under one name. Arrays are the whole of the next lesson. For now it is enough that `foreach` walks through one, exactly as it walks through the characters of a string.
C# gathers the loose arguments into the array for you. That is the only thing `params` does.

steps.explain: The longest of the four words is `not`, with 3 letters. With no arguments the array is empty, the loop body never runs, and `best` is still 0.

steps.title: Returning two things: tuples
body: `return` hands back one value. When a method naturally has two results and neither is a pass/fail flag, bundle them in a **tuple**: several values in one pair of parentheses.
(int min, int max) Order(int a, int b)
The return type `(int min, int max)` lists the parts and names them. The caller has two ways to get at them:
var (low, high) = Order(8, 3);  // unpack into two variables
The second form is called **deconstruction**. It is usually the tidiest.

steps.prompt: Match each piece of syntax to what it gives you.
pairs: the caller may leave this argument out
says which parameter the value is for
a second result the method must assign
the method can read and change the caller's variable
the caller may pass any number of arguments

steps.title: Sidekick piece: minute stats and the estimate parser
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** `sk add "Fix login" --est 1h30` and `sk stats` need two methods. Each uses a parameter feature from this lesson.

**1.** `static (int Min, int Max, int Total) MinuteStats(params int[] minutes)` returns the smallest, the largest and the total of **any number** of minute counts. With no values at all it returns `(0, 0, 0)`.

**2.** `static bool TryParseMinutes(string text, out int minutes)` reads an estimate the way people type it. Ignore case and spaces. Hours are a number before `h`; minutes are a number after it (or the whole text), optionally ending in `m`. It returns `true` and sets `minutes`, or returns `false` (with `minutes` = 0) for anything else.
`text.IndexOf('h')` finds the `h` (or -1), `Substring` cuts, and `int.TryParse` refuses anything that is not a number.
starter: static (int Min, int Max, int Total) MinuteStats(params int[] minutes)
static bool TryParseMinutes(string text, out int minutes)
solution: static (int Min, int Max, int Total) MinuteStats(params int[] minutes)
int min = minutes[0], max = minutes[0], total = 0;
static bool TryParseMinutes(string text, out int minutes)
if (!int.TryParse(t.Substring(0, h), out hours) || hours < 0) return false;
if (t.Length > 0 && (!int.TryParse(t, out mins) || mins < 0)) return false;
template: (bool, int) dojoParse(string s) { bool ok = TryParseMinutes(s, out int m); return (ok, m); }
hints: `MinuteStats`: return `(0, 0, 0)` for an empty array first; then start min and max at `minutes[0]` and walk the array.
`TryParseMinutes`: clean up with `text.Trim().ToLower().Replace(" ", "")`. If there is an `h`, parse the part before it as hours and keep the part after it.
Then drop one trailing `m`, and parse what is left as minutes (an empty rest is fine only if there was an `h`). Any failed `int.TryParse` or negative number: `return false`.
steps.explain: `params` lets callers write `MinuteStats(45, 120, 30)` without building an array, a named tuple returns three answers at once, and `out` hands back a value next to the true/false. Sidekick uses all three.

build.unlocks: `sk add --est 1h30` understands estimates, and `sk stats` has its numbers.
